nameStory: This lichen gets its "lung" name from its thin, papery lobes that flutter and breathe in the wind like lung tissue. The "textured" part refers to its distinctively pitted and bumpy surface that feels like rough sandpaper when dry. Early botanists thought its respiratory-like appearance was fitting for a species that literally breathes through its surface!
description: Textured Lung Lichen is a large, leafy lichen that forms spectacular rosettes up to 8 inches across on tree trunks and rocks. Its thin, papery lobes are gray-green when dry and bright green when wet, with a distinctively pitted and textured upper surface that sets it apart from smoother lung lichens. The lobes overlap like shingles and often have a slightly crispy texture that makes a soft rustling sound when touched.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Upper surface is distinctly pitted and bumpy, feeling like coarse sandpaper when dry - much rougher than other lung lichens

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Large, leafy (foliose) lobes that overlap like roof shingles, forming circular rosettes up to 8 inches across

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Gray-green to brownish when dry, transforming to vibrant bright green when wet - the color change is dramatic and immediate

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost exclusively grows on tree bark, especially preferring the rough bark of older maples, oaks, and ash trees

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: One of the larger foliose lichens in New England - mature specimens can cover areas the size of a dinner plate

habitat: Textured Lung Lichen thrives in humid, mature hardwood forests throughout New England, particularly in areas with clean air and consistent moisture. Look for it on the trunks of older maple, oak, and ash trees in well-established forests, usually 3-10 feet up from the ground. It's most abundant in mountainous regions and river valleys where morning mist and fog provide regular moisture.

seasonality.spring: Most vibrant after spring rains when the bright green wet coloration shows beautifully against dark bark. New growth edges may be visible on established specimens.
seasonality.summer: Often appears grayish and dormant during dry spells, but transforms dramatically after summer thunderstorms. The textured surface is most apparent when specimens are dry.
seasonality.fall: Excellent time for identification as the lichen contrasts beautifully with colorful autumn leaves. Specimens are often well-hydrated from fall rains and show their best green coloration.
seasonality.winter: Visible year-round and often at its most textured appearance when dry. Snow melt and winter rains can trigger the dramatic color transformation from gray to green.

funFact: Despite looking delicate and papery, Textured Lung Lichen can survive being completely dried out for months, then come back to life and resume photosynthesis within minutes of getting wet - faster than you can make a cup of coffee!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Smooth Lung Lichen (Lobaria pulmonaria), but the textured surface is the dead giveaway - if it feels rough and pitted like sandpaper, you've found the textured species. Memory trick: "Textured feels textured, smooth feels smooth!"
contextualKnowledge: The genus name Lobarina means "little lobe," though there's nothing little about this impressive lichen! It's considered an indicator species for old-growth forest conditions and clean air, so finding it suggests you're in a healthy, well-preserved woodland ecosystem.
compareHints: Textured Lung Lichen is actually the only Lobarina species in New England, making it unique in its genus here. It's most similar to species in the related genus Lobaria, but can be distinguished by its smaller, more textured lobes and preference for drier bark surfaces. Unlike the massive Tree Lungwort (Lobaria pulmonaria), it rarely develops the bright green soredia patches on its surface.
